name: Hardware Simulation / Synthesis Mismatch
description:
The hardware design contains structures that are interpreted
		differently during synthesis than during simulation, which
		cause inconsistencies in security-relevant behavior between
		the synthesized implementation and the simulation.

note:
<xhtml:p>This weakness can be introduced when HDL
			constructs, assignment ordering, synthesis directives, or
			tool-dependent semantics are used whose simulation
			behavior may not match synthesis interpretation. These
			constructs may behave correctly during HDL simulation but
			produce different security-relevant behavior in the
			synthesized implementation.</xhtml:p>

<xhtml:p>This weakness can be introduced or exposed during
			synthesis when the synthesis tool applies assumptions,
			optimizations, or transformations to HDL structures that
			cannot be physically implemented exactly as the simulation
			semantics dictate, or that permit multiple (valid)
			hardware implementations. The resulting netlist may behave
			differently from the model that was verified during
			simulation.</xhtml:p>

common_consequences.note:
<xhtml:p>The consequences depend on the affected hardware
			behavior. The synthesized implementation may make
			different control decisions, incorrectly update protected
			state, expose data, or fail to enforce restrictions that
			appeared to operate correctly during HDL
			simulation.</xhtml:p>

description:
<xhtml:p>Establish and enforce HDL coding and review
			practices that minimize differences between simulation
			semantics and synthesis interpretation. Avoid HDL
			constructs, synthesis directives, and tool-dependent
			behaviors known to cause simulation/synthesis mismatch,
			with particular attention to security-relevant
			logic.</xhtml:p>
potential_mitigations.effectiveness_notes:
<xhtml:p>Avoidance of the patterns of code which can
			result in these errors removes the opportunity for
			error. However, in some cases (notably state machine
			encodings) this can be very difficult to achieve
			efficiently.</xhtml:p>

description:
<xhtml:p>For security-critical logic, preserve intentional
			redundancy that is required for security. Examples may
			include redundant logic, triple modular redundancy (TMR)
			structures, Hamming-distance state encodings, or
			state-machine recovery logic. Use synthesis constraints,
			preservation attributes, carefully controlled structural
			implementation, or manual implementation of selected
			critical blocks to prevent this redundancy from being
			merged, re-encoded, or optimized away.</xhtml:p>
potential_mitigations.effectiveness_notes:
<xhtml:p>This mitigation removes the structures which
			cause the problem, at the expense of additional design and
			verification effort, and additional risk of inclusion of
			other functional errors.</xhtml:p>

detection_methods.description:
<xhtml:p>HDL linting, rule-based static analysis, and HDL
			checker tools can examine source code for structures that
			may be interpreted differently by simulation and synthesis
			tools. They may identify synthesis-sensitive coding
			patterns associated with this weakness.</xhtml:p>
detection_methods.effectiveness_notes:
<xhtml:p>This method can be useful for detecting potential
			coding issues, but it may not reveal whether these
			constructs result in observable behavioral divergence
			after synthesis. Moreover, a user may suppress or bypass
			these warnings and still produce the erroneous synthesized
			hardware implementation. This method can give false
			positives.</xhtml:p>

detection_methods.description:
<xhtml:p>Synthesis warning review can examine synthesis
			logs and reports for tool messages associated with
			possible simulation/synthesis mismatch. It may identify
			ignored constructs, unsupported HDL semantics, synthesis
			assumptions, or optimizations that could affect
			security-relevant behavior.</xhtml:p>
detection_methods.effectiveness_notes:
<xhtml:p>Can reveal potential synthesis issues but relies
			on engineers interpreting warnings. Moreover, a user may
			suppress or bypass these warnings and still produce the
			erroneous synthesized hardware implementation.</xhtml:p>

detection_methods.description:
<xhtml:p>HDL-source-to-netlist formal equivalence checking
			can examine the simulated model and synthesized netlist
			for behavioral mismatch associated with this weakness. It
			may identify non-equivalent outputs, failed
			compare-points, state-mapping issues, or counterexamples
			under the checked constraints.</xhtml:p>
detection_methods.effectiveness_notes:
<xhtml:p>Formal equivalence checking can be effective at
			the IP level for identifying mismatches between the
			source-code model and synthesized implementation. However,
			effectiveness may decrease as design complexity grows,
			particularly at the SoC level, due to state-space
			expansion and difficulty mapping non-equivalent
			points. Synthesis optimizations may merge, eliminate, or
			rename signals, which can also produce false positives or
			require additional setup to account for expected
			transformations.</xhtml:p>

detection_methods.description:
<xhtml:p>Cross-simulation across HDL-source and
			post-synthesis models can examine both abstraction levels
			for observable behavioral divergence associated with this
			weakness. It may identify mismatches when
			security-relevant behaviors are explicitly
			exercised.</xhtml:p>
detection_methods.effectiveness_notes:
<xhtml:p>This method can be useful for detecting
			observable behavioral mismatches, but it may not exercise
			all execution scenarios and should be combined with other
			detection methods to improve coverage.</xhtml:p>

detection_methods.description:
<xhtml:p>Coverage-guided differential fuzzing can examine
			HDL source code and synthesized implementation models for
			behavioral divergence associated with this weakness. It
			may identify generated inputs or state conditions that
			expose synthesis-induced mismatches.</xhtml:p>
detection_methods.effectiveness_notes:
<xhtml:p>This method can be useful for detecting
			previously unknown synthesis-induced behavioral mismatches
			by exploring diverse execution paths through
			coverage-guided input generation. However, it may not
			exercise every reachable design state and should be
			combined with other detection methods to improve
			coverage.</xhtml:p>

mapping_notes.rationale: This CWE entry is at the Base level of abstraction, which is a preferred level of abstraction for mapping to the root causes of vulnerabilities.
mapping_notes.comments:
Since this entry is often resultant, there might be
        other CWEs that are more appropriate as the root cause,
        although there might be some gaps.  Carefully read both the
        name and description to ensure that this mapping is an
        appropriate fit. Do not try to 'force' a mapping to a
        lower-level Base/Variant simply to comply with this preferred
        level of abstraction.
